fetched_contents.text: Compare Battery-Electric & Hydrogen Buses: Emissions & Range from Transfinder Image Credit: Adam E Moreira / Wikimedia Commons The debate between battery-electric and hydrogen fuel cell technology for buses has been ongoing for years, with both sides having strong proponents. However, in recent years it seems that the pendulum has swung more in favor of battery-electric technology due to its falling costs and increasing efficiency. But overall, your best choice depends on the features you prioritize in a vehicle. Battery electric vehicles (BEVs), also known as all-electric cars, are powered by electricity from batteries. BEVs have become increasingly popular in recent years due to advances in battery technology and the desire to reduce dependence on fossil fuels. There are different BEVs, including those with range extenders and those without. Range extenders are small gasoline engines that generate electricity to extend the range of the BEV beyond what the battery alone would allow. BEVs without range extenders are sometimes referred to as pure electric vehicles (PEV). The advantages of BEVs over traditional gasoline-powered cars are their much lower emissions, particularly greenhouse gases like carbon dioxide; their significantly cheaper operating costs; and, for some drivers, the feeling of increased power and torque. Image Credit: CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons Hydrogen Fuel Cell Buses Hydrogen fuel cell buses have recently gained popularity as a clean and efficient alternative to traditional diesel-powered buses. Fuel cells convert chemical energy into electrical energy, with water and heat as the only byproducts, making them much cleaner than internal combustion engines, which produce harmful emissions like carbon dioxide and nitrogen oxides. Fuel cell buses are also more efficient than diesel buses, meaning they use less fuel to travel the same distance. That results in significant cost savings for bus operators and reduced environmental impact. Efficiency Comparison Energy Efficiency The battery-electric bus is more efficient than the hydrogen fuel cell bus in terms of overall energy efficiency. The difference is that the battery-electric bus uses a single energy source (electricity) to power its motor. In contrast, the hydrogen fuel cell bus relies on two energy sources (hydrogen and oxygen) to generate electricity to power its motor. The overall efficiency of a battery-electric bus is about 85-90%, while the overall efficiency of a hydrogen fuel cell bus is only about 60-70%. It means that, for every 100 units of energy input, a battery-electric bus will use about 85-90 units of that energy to move the vehicle, while a hydrogen fuel cell bus will only use about 60-70 units of that energy to move the vehicle. Carbon Dioxide Emissions The battery-electric bus is also more efficient than the hydrogen fuel cell bus in carbon dioxide emissions. The reason for this is that, while both buses produce emissions when operating, the battery-electric bus emits no gas when it is not running (i.e., when it is plugged into the grid). On the other hand, the hydrogen fuel cell bus produces emissions even when it is not being used, as a result of the need to constantly replenish its supply of hydrogen. Evidence on how hydrogen bus TCO changed over time and whether it declined, stabilized, or increased

The evidence across 2015–2021 is thin and mostly indirect, with only a few sources suggesting TCO trends and others emphasizing uncertainty. For the historical period, one source notes that hydrogen pathways showed 14–31% higher total cost of ownership than their diesel counterpart, with the highest value of AU$5.60/km by grid [N4-R2]. Another source from the same period reports that hydrogen buses still have a much higher maintenance burden than diesel and battery electric buses, with California data showing 50% more maintenance than diesel and 100% more than battery electric [N4-R4]. These results imply that early TCO estimates were relatively unfavorable compared to diesel and, especially, electric alternatives, but they do not provide a clear 2015–2021 timeline.

For recent estimates from 2022–2025, the evidence becomes more explicit but still mixed. A 2023 study on hydrogen fuel cell electric buses carried out sensitivity and probabilistic analyses to assess total cost of ownership [N1-R2][N2-R4]. Another 2023 study similarly conducted comprehensive examination with sensitivity and probabilistic analyses [N1-R4][N2-R4]. These studies suggest that TCO modeling is increasingly sophisticated, but the excerpts do not give specific numeric values for 2022–2025. A 2023 report on hydrogen buses also shows that sales grew significantly, with a 72.3% increase from 2022, and mentions subsidies for commercial vehicles utilizing hydrogen [N2-R2]. This indicates market movement, but not necessarily a clear TCO decline.

For 2030–2035 projections, the evidence points to a conditional and uncertain future. One 2025 report states that hydrogen buses until 2030 still have 15.4% higher TCO than diesel bus systems, even under a hypothetical scaling-up effect of hydrogen [N3-R3]. A 2024 Lawrence Transit Study report mentions fixed cumulative TCO costs for 2024–2035 but notes that the small number of FCEBs in Scenario 3 makes the result qualitative rather than quantitative [N3-R5]. A 2025 study on hydrogen bus market growth suggests the U.S. market could reach USD 1.5 billion by 2035 [N5-R3], but that is market valuation, not TCO. A 2025 report on fuel cell electric vehicles also forecasts adoption through 2045, but again does not provide TCO numbers [N2-R5].

Overall, the trend appears to be mixed rather than clearly downward: early TCOs were relatively high, and the evidence does not establish a consistent decline across 2015–2035. Instead, the data suggest that TCO could stabilize or even rise if hydrogen price volatility, infrastructure costs, and scale effects remain unfavorable, while it could fall if production and distribution costs decline substantially and deployment scales. Another source highlights that hydrogen fuel remains costly, comparing it to electric buses and noting that subsidies are still needed [N2-R2][N6-R4]. Fuel price volatility is therefore likely to keep TCO unstable, especially if hydrogen prices fluctuate or remain high relative to alternatives.

The evidence emphasizes that hydrogen infrastructure is expensive to build and maintain, and that the market is still developing [N2-R2][N6-F1]. Hydrogen buses compare unfavorably to battery buses in the evidence provided. A comparative TCO analysis states that hydrogen buses until 2030 still have 15.4% higher TCO than diesel bus systems, and that battery buses are much cheaper to operate and maintain than hydrogen counterparts [N3-R3][N6-R4]. Another source notes that battery-electric buses are more efficient than hydrogen fuel cell buses in terms of energy efficiency and carbon dioxide emissions, and that hydrogen fuel remains costly [N6-R2][N6-R4]. A broader comparison in the evidence also says that BEBs are more efficient and emit less pollution than hydrogen fuel cell buses, and that battery-electric buses are cheaper to operate and maintain [N6-F1]. These comparisons suggest that, relative to battery buses, hydrogen buses face a significant TCO disadvantage unless hydrogen prices fall sharply and infrastructure costs decline substantially.

### 2) What assumptions about hydrogen production and use define the TCO
The evidence also shows that the TCO of hydrogen buses depends heavily on assumptions about hydrogen production and use. One source explicitly states that hydrogen pathways showed 14–31% higher total cost of ownership than diesel [N4-R2]. Another source emphasizes that hydrogen fuel remains costly and that subsidies are still needed [N2-R2]. A 2023 study on hydrogen buses carried out sensitivity and probabilistic analysis, which is directly relevant because hydrogen production, distribution, and price assumptions are likely to drive the TCO result [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The 2025 market report also notes that growth is driven by zero-emission vehicle demand and supportive government policies [N5-R4], which indirectly shows how production and use assumptions are tied to the TCO outlook.

### 3) Limits of the evidence and where uncertainty remains
The limits of the evidence are considerable. First, the evidence is uneven: historical TCO ranges are indirect, recent studies emphasize sensitivity analysis without specific numeric values, and long-term projections are scenario-dependent [N1-R2][N1-R4][N3-R5]. Second, the comparisons are often relative rather than absolute, so conclusions about hydrogen buses must be interpreted in relation to diesel and battery buses rather than as isolated claims [N3-R3][N6-R3][N6-F1]. Third, assumptions about hydrogen production, infrastructure, and deployment are central, but the evidence does not consistently quantify them across studies [N4-R2][N5-R4][N1-R2]. Finally, the evidence suggests that TCO is highly sensitive to scale and market conditions, so a single headline conclusion is difficult [N3-R5][N5-R3].

## Data quality and assumptions underlying hydrogen bus TCO studies

### 1) Study scope and geographic/regional specificity
Study scope and geographic/regional specificity are important. The evidence shows that studies vary by region and by vehicle class. One comparative TCO analysis focuses on public transport systems in small to midsize cities [N6-R1]. Another hydrogen bus market report notes the U.S. market [N5-R3], while another hydrogen bus market report is global [N5-R1]. A 2024 Lawrence Transit Study report explicitly mentions fixed cumulative TCO costs for 2024–2035, but the small number of FCEBs in Scenario 3 suggests that regional or fleet-specific assumptions can make results less generalizable [N3-R5]. This geographic and regional specificity means that a TCO estimate for one city or country may not apply directly to another.

### 2) Assumptions about hydrogen production and distribution
Assumptions about hydrogen production and distribution are central to TCO modeling. The evidence repeatedly shows that hydrogen pathways have higher TCO than diesel, and that hydrogen fuel remains costly [N4-R2][N2-R2]. A 2023 study on hydrogen buses explicitly used sensitivity and probabilistic analysis, indicating that hydrogen production, distribution, and price assumptions are treated as uncertain inputs [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The same study also discusses hydrogen-assumptions in an annex, reinforcing that production and distribution assumptions are not fixed [N7-R2]. The 2025 market report also notes that growth is driven by zero-emission vehicle demand and supportive government policies, which implies that hydrogen supply chain assumptions are tied to market development rather than fixed technology [N5-R4]. Overall, TCO studies are highly sensitive to whether hydrogen is produced locally, imported, or distributed through a mature network.

### 3) Sensitivity and probabilistic analysis details
Sensitivity and probabilistic analysis details are a major methodological feature. The evidence shows that several studies carry out comprehensive examinations with sensitivity and probabilistic analysis [N1-R2][N1-R4]. One study explicitly mentions sensitivity and probabilistic analyses in the title and annex [N7-R2]. Another study similarly uses sensitivity and probabilistic analysis to assess total cost of ownership [N1-R4][N2-R4]. These methods are important because they show that TCO is not treated as a single point estimate but as a range of possible outcomes. However, the evidence does not provide detailed methodological breakdowns, so the extent of uncertainty remains partly opaque [N1-R2][N1-R4][N7-R2].

### 4) How assumptions affect the projected TCO trend
How assumptions affect the projected TCO trend is clear. The evidence suggests that assumptions about hydrogen production and distribution can shift TCO substantially. For example, a 2023 study found that hydrogen pathways had 14–31% higher total cost of ownership than diesel [N4-R2], while another study noted that hydrogen buses require dedicated infrastructure for refueling, which can be expensive to build and maintain [N6-F1]. The 2024 Lawrence Transit Study report also shows that small fleet size and limited deployment can make TCO results qualitative [N3-R5]. In other words, if hydrogen production costs fall, infrastructure costs decline, and deployment scales, TCO can improve. If those assumptions do not hold, TCO remains high. The evidence therefore supports a conditional rather than a deterministic conclusion: TCO trends depend heavily on the assumptions underlying the study [N4-R2][N6-F1][N3-R5][N1-R2][N1-R4].

## Bottom line
The evidence supports a cautious conclusion: hydrogen bus TCO has been relatively high relative to diesel and battery buses in the historical period, and the trend from 2015 to 2035 is conditional rather than clearly downward. The main drivers are hydrogen price volatility, infrastructure cost declines with scale, vehicle cost reductions as technology matures, and maintenance burden relative to diesel and electric buses [N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R1][N4-R5]. Policy incentives, market growth, and supply chain development can improve the outlook, but slow deployment, high production costs, and continued price volatility can keep TCO high [N5-R2][N2-R2][N5-R4][N5-R3][N2-R5]. Overall, the most defensible conclusion is that hydrogen buses may become more cost-competitive over time, but only under favorable assumptions, and the evidence base remains limited and scenario-dependent [N1-R2][N1-R4][N3-R5][N5-R4].

Main factors driving hydrogen bus TCO changes

Fuel cost changes and hydrogen price volatility are a central driver. The evidence indicates that hydrogen buses depend heavily on the cost of hydrogen, with one source noting that hydrogen pathways had 14–31% higher total cost of ownership than diesel [N4-R2]. Another source highlights that hydrogen fuel remains costly, comparing it to electric buses and noting that subsidies are still needed [N2-R2][N6-R4]. Fuel price volatility is therefore likely to keep TCO unstable, especially if hydrogen prices fluctuate or remain high relative to alternatives.

Infrastructure cost declines and scale effects are another major factor. The evidence emphasizes that hydrogen infrastructure is expensive to build and maintain, and that the market is still developing [N2-R2][N6-F1]. However, the same sources also suggest that scale can reduce costs, including through network effects and broader hydrogen supply chain development. A 2023 study explicitly used sensitivity and probabilistic analysis to assess total cost of ownership, implying that infrastructure and distribution assumptions are central to the TCO calculation [N1-R2][N1-R4]. The 2024 Lawrence Transit Study report further notes that fixed cumulative TCO costs for 2024–2035 are reported, but the small fleet size in one scenario indicates that scale matters [N3-R5]. So, as deployment grows and infrastructure becomes more established, TCO could stabilize or decline, but only if scale effects outweigh initial capital costs.

Vehicle cost reductions and technology maturity are also important. The evidence suggests that vehicle costs have been a major part of TCO, especially because the hydrogen bus market is still relatively new [N2-R2][N5-R3]. A 2023 study on hydrogen buses shows significant market growth and mentions subsidies for commercial vehicles, which can reduce the effective vehicle price [N2-R2]. The 2023 study on fuel cell electric buses also used sensitivity and probabilistic analysis, which is relevant because technology maturity affects both initial purchase cost and operational reliability [N1-R2][N1-R4]. In other words, as hydrogen bus technology matures, vehicle costs may fall, and TCO could improve.

Maintenance cost trends and operational complexity are another key factor. The evidence is more mixed here, but clearly unfavorable in some respects. One source says maintenance costs for hydrogen buses fall between diesel and electric at approximately $0.35 per mile [N4-R1]. Another source reports that hydrogen buses require 50% more maintenance than diesel and 100% more than battery electric buses [N4-R4]. A lifecycle-cost perspective also notes that overall expenses include maintenance and depreciation [N4-R5]. The evidence across 2015–2021 is thin and mostly indirect, with only a few sources suggesting TCO trends and others emphasizing uncertainty. A 2023 study on hydrogen fuel cell electric buses carried out sensitivity and probabilistic analyses to assess total cost of ownership [N1-R2][N2-R4]. Overall, TCO studies are highly sensitive to whether hydrogen is produced locally, imported, or distributed through a mature network.

### 3) Sensitivity and probabilistic analysis details
Sensitivity and probabilistic analysis details are a major methodological feature. The evidence shows that several studies carry out comprehensive examinations with sensitivity and probabilistic analysis [N1-R2][N1-R4]. One study explicitly mentions sensitivity and probabilistic analyses in the title and annex [N7-R2]. Another study similarly uses sensitivity and probabilistic analysis to assess total cost of ownership [N1-R4][N2-R4]. These methods are important because they show that TCO is not treated as a single point estimate but as a range of possible outcomes. However, the evidence does not provide detailed methodological breakdowns, so the extent of uncertainty remains partly opaque [N1-R2][N1-R4][N7-R2].

### 4) How assumptions affect the projected TCO trend
How assumptions affect the projected TCO trend is clear. The evidence suggests that assumptions about hydrogen production and distribution can shift TCO substantially. For example, a 2023 study found that hydrogen pathways had 14–31% higher total cost of ownership than diesel [N4-R2], while another study noted that hydrogen buses require dedicated infrastructure for refueling, which can be expensive to build and maintain [N6-F1]. The 2024 Lawrence Transit Study report also shows that small fleet size and limited deployment can make TCO results qualitative [N3-R5]. In other words, if hydrogen production costs fall, infrastructure costs decline, and deployment scales, TCO can improve. If those assumptions do not hold, TCO remains high. The evidence therefore supports a conditional rather than a deterministic conclusion: TCO trends depend heavily on the assumptions underlying the study [N4-R2][N6-F1][N3-R5][N1-R2][N1-R4].

## Bottom line
The evidence supports a cautious conclusion: hydrogen bus TCO has been relatively high relative to diesel and battery buses in the historical period, and the trend from 2015 to 2035 is conditional rather than clearly downward. The main drivers are hydrogen price volatility, infrastructure cost declines with scale, vehicle cost reductions as technology matures, and maintenance burden relative to diesel and electric buses [N4-R2][N4-R4][N4-R1][N4-R5]. Policy incentives, market growth, and supply chain development can improve the outlook, but slow deployment, high production costs, and continued price volatility can keep TCO high [N5-R2][N2-R2][N5-R4][N5-R3][N2-R5]. Overall, the most defensible conclusion is that hydrogen buses may become more cost-competitive over time, but only under favorable assumptions, and the evidence base remains limited and scenario-dependent [N1-R2][N1-R4][N3-R5][N5-R4].
